1000967.etyen:
Borrowed from English Titania, the name of the fairy queen in William Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Shakespeare took the name from Latin tītānia, the feminine of tītānius (“of or pertaining to the Titans”), from Tītān (“Titan”). In Ovid's works, the Latin form was used as an epithet for female descendants of the Titans, including Diana.
The moon of Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1787 and was named after Shakespeare's Titania. The asteroid 593 Titania was likewise named after the Shakespearean character.

1005063.etyen:
An orthographic variant of Bodhild, distinguished by the doubled final -ll. The source name Bodhild is a Danish-influenced variant of Bothild and ultimately continues Old Norse Bóthildr.
The Old Norse name is formed from bót (“remedy, help, improvement”) and hildr (“battle, fight”), literally “remedy-battle”. The first element is from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“improvement, betterment; recompense, atonement”), while the second element is from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle, fight”).
